script.opening: "I keep getting nosebleeds, doctor — several over the past few weeks. The last one was a real worry, it wouldn’t stop for a good twenty minutes and there was a fair bit of blood. I’m on a blood thinner, apixaban, for my irregular heartbeat — atrial fibrillation — and I take tablets for blood pressure. Should I be concerned?"

facts.text: Five in the past 4 weeks, both sides at different times. Most stopped within 5–10 minutes. The last one, 3 days ago, took about 20 minutes and soaked a tea towel. Some ran down his throat. Not bleeding now; feels fine.
Tipped his head back and held the bony top of his nose, letting go every minute or so "to see if it had stopped".

No blocked nose on one side, no blood-stained discharge, no facial pain or swelling, no loose teeth, no lumps in the neck. No bruising elsewhere, no blood in urine or stools, no gum bleeding. No family history of bleeding problems or nosebleeds.
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily (for 2 years); amlodipine 10 mg. No aspirin or anti-inflammatories. No allergies. Kidneys "checked last year, fine I think".
Has a home monitor: "usually about 150 over 90 — the nurse wanted it lower". Took it this morning: 156/92, pulse irregular about 80.
Central heating on a lot, nose feels dry and crusty. Picks at crusts. Weight about 85 kg; no recent weight change.
Retired postman. Lives with his wife, Joan. Drives. Drinks 2 pints at the weekend. Ex-smoker.

Calm but quietly anxious. You haven’t stopped the apixaban and want to know if you should. If asked to show how you stop a nosebleed, demonstrate the wrong way (head back, pinching the bony bridge). Then copy the correct way when taught: "Like this? Lean forward, pinch here, don’t let go."

ice.ideas: "Maybe it’s the blood thinner. Or something wrong inside."
ice.concerns: "With the thinners, I worry one day it won’t stop." His brother-in-law had "a growth in the nose" (only if worries are explored).
ice.expectations: "To know whether I should worry, whether to stop the thinner, and how to stop them."

cues: "I held the top of my nose and kept letting go" — first aid to correct.
"Should I stop the blood thinner?" — needs review, not stopping on impulse.
"The nurse wanted it lower" (if blood pressure is asked) — uncontrolled hypertension to address.

checkpoints.text: Teaches correct EPISTAXIS FIRST-AID — sit forward, pinch the SOFT part of the nose continuously for 10–15 minutes, lean forward/spit out blood, a cold pack on the bridge, avoid lying back/sniffing

Recognises most bleeds are anterior/benign but REVIEWS the ANTICOAGULATION (which drug, indication, dose/renal function for a DOAC, control — INR if warfarin, balance of risks, without stopping it on impulse) and antiplatelets/NSAIDs, and the HYPERTENSION (NICE NG136)

Knows the ESCALATION/admission criteria — bleeding not controlled by two rounds of 10–15 minutes’ correct pressure, heavy/posterior bleeding, haemodynamic compromise, significant bleeding while anticoagulated

Knows primary-care treatment (topical antiseptic cream, nasal cautery of a visible anterior point by a trained clinician after face-to-face rhinoscopy) and ENT referral for recurrent/refractory epistaxis
Considers RED FLAGS — persistent unilateral bleeding/obstruction or a nasal mass (sinonasal tumour → ENT), and bleeding disorder/HHT — referring appropriately
Addresses his worry about the bleeding and the blood thinners, reassures proportionately, and checks understanding of first-aid
Advises PREVENTION (humidification/saline/emollient, avoid picking/forceful blowing) and arranges anticoagulation/BP review

Safety-nets and follows up: when to seek urgent/emergency care (uncontrolled/heavy/posterior bleeding, feeling faint), ENT referral for recurrence, red-flag awareness (unilateral/mass), and anticoagulation/BP review — first-aid + medication review + escalation criteria

worked.txt: "Most nosebleeds come from the front of the nose and are not dangerous, even on blood thinners — but you need the right first-aid, which a lot of people get wrong. Sit up, lean FORWARD, and pinch the SOFT part of your nose firmly for a full 10–15 minutes WITHOUT letting go to check. Spit out any blood, don’t tip your head back. A cold pack on the bridge of your nose may help."

"Being on blood thinners makes bleeds last longer, so let’s review them — you take apixaban for your atrial fibrillation, so I’ll check the reason still stands, that the dose is right for your age, weight and kidney tests, and any other tablets that thin the blood; apixaban doesn’t need INR checks the way warfarin does. Please keep taking it meanwhile — any change I’d discuss with your heart team. And let’s make sure your blood pressure is well controlled, as that can contribute."

"Go to A&E — or call 999 if you feel unwell — if a bleed won’t stop after two rounds of 10–15 minutes of proper pressure, if blood is pouring down the back of your throat, or if you feel faint or dizzy. Those need hospital, sometimes packing."

"For the recurrent bleeds, I’d like to see you in person to check your pulse and blood pressure and look in your nose and, if there’s an obvious vessel at the front, cauterise it, and a cream can reduce crusting and re-bleeding. If they keep happening, I’ll refer you to ENT."
"Just to be safe — are the bleeds always the same nostril, with a blocked feeling on that side? … No, both sides. Good — persistent one-sided bleeding or blockage is the thing I’d want ENT to check."

"To prevent them: a saline spray or a dab of emollient inside the nose for dryness, and avoid picking or hard blowing. Come back if they keep recurring, become one-sided, or you ever can’t stop one — and we’ll review your blood thinners together."

f.learning: EPISTAXIS management starts with correct FIRST-AID: sit up and lean FORWARD (not back), pinch the SOFT part of the nose (not the bony bridge) firmly and continuously for 10–15 minutes without releasing to check, breathe through the mouth and spit out blood (don’t swallow), and a cold pack on the bridge of the nose may help — avoiding lying back, sniffing or blowing afterwards. Most nosebleeds are ANTERIOR (Little’s area) and benign (nose-picking, dryness, trauma, URTIs), but in an anticoagulated/antiplatelet patient REVIEW the anticoagulation (which drug, indication, DOAC dose against weight and renal function, interacting drugs, control — INR if on warfarin, balance of risks; BNF), without stopping it on impulse (a shared decision with the prescriber), and the HYPERTENSION (optimise per NICE NG136). Know the ESCALATION/admission criteria: bleeding not controlled by 10–15 minutes of correct pressure repeated once, heavy or POSTERIOR bleeding (blood pouring down the throat, no visible anterior source), haemodynamic compromise (dizziness, tachycardia, hypotension), or significant bleeding while anticoagulated — posterior/uncontrolled bleeds need ENT/emergency care (packing). In primary care, examine face to face (pulse, BP, anterior rhinoscopy) and treat an anterior bleeding point with topical antiseptic cream (e.g. Naseptin, dose per BNF) and/or, by a trained clinician, nasal CAUTERY (silver nitrate) of a visible vessel, and refer to ENT for recurrent/refractory epistaxis. Keep RED FLAGS in mind: persistent UNILATERAL nasal bleeding/obstruction or a nasal MASS (possible sinonasal tumour → ENT), and features of a bleeding disorder (FBC and clotting) or hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasia, family history; Curaçao criteria, international HHT guidelines 2020). Advise prevention (nasal humidification/saline/emollient, avoid picking/forceful blowing) and arrange anticoagulation/BP review. The skill is correct first-aid + anticoagulation/BP review + escalation criteria + red-flag awareness.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG136 (hypertension in adults) · [2] Curaçao criteria for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Shovlin et al., 2000, international) · [3] Second international HHT guidelines (Faughnan et al., Ann Intern Med 2020, international)
knowledge.summary: Most recurrent nosebleeds come from Little’s area at the front of the septum and are benign, but anticoagulation makes them last longer. Teach first aid properly, review the anticoagulant and blood pressure without stopping the anticoagulant on impulse, treat a visible anterior vessel, and know when to send to hospital. Keep one-sided bleeding with obstruction, and HHT, in mind.

points.t: Sit up and lean forward, mouth open. Pinch the soft, fleshy part of the nose (not the bony bridge) firmly and continuously for 10–15 minutes without letting go to check. Spit out blood rather than swallow it. A cold pack on the bridge may help. Afterwards avoid blowing, picking, straining, heavy lifting and hot drinks for a day or so.

The large majority arise anteriorly from Little’s area. Triggers include dryness, picking, trauma and colds. Posterior bleeds are more likely in older people, those on anticoagulants and those with hypertension: blood pouring down the throat, bleeding from both nostrils, or no visible anterior source.

Same-day emergency care (999 if unwell) if bleeding continues despite 10–15 minutes of correct pressure repeated once, is heavy or posterior, or there are signs of shock: pallor, sweating, dizziness, faintness, fast pulse, low blood pressure. A low threshold applies when anticoagulated.

points.h: Review the anticoagulant, don’t just stop it
points.t: Check the indication and whether it is still needed, the dose against current weight and renal function (DOACs), interacting drugs (antiplatelets, NSAIDs), and INR if on warfarin. Stopping or pausing an anticoagulant is a shared decision with the prescriber or specialist, weighed against stroke or clot risk.
Measure BP. Hypertension is associated with epistaxis severity; optimise control per NICE NG136 [1]. A very high reading during a bleed may partly reflect distress; recheck.

If a bleeding point is visible anteriorly and the clinician is trained, silver nitrate cautery to one side of the septum. Chlorhexidine with neomycin nasal cream reduces crusting and re-bleeding (dose per BNF; Naseptin contains arachis oil, so check for peanut or soya allergy). Refer to ENT when bleeds keep recurring despite this, or no source is seen.

Persistent one-sided bleeding with nasal obstruction, blood-stained discharge, facial pain or swelling, or a visible mass: refer urgently to ENT to exclude a sinonasal tumour. Easy bruising or other bleeding: FBC and clotting. HHT: recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds, telangiectasia on lips, tongue or fingers, and a first-degree relative with HHT [2][3].

Treat dryness (saline spray, a thin smear of petroleum jelly or emollient inside the nostril, humidifying the room), stop picking and forceful blowing, and address contributing medicines such as NSAIDs.

Pulse and BP; anterior rhinoscopy for a bleeding point; FBC and renal function (apixaban dosing) as indicated; INR only if on warfarin.
Anterior Little’s area bleed versus posterior bleed, anticoagulant effect, hypertension, bleeding disorder, HHT, sinonasal tumour.
Screened shock, one-sided obstruction or discharge, bleeding elsewhere and HHT features.
Recurrent anterior epistaxis made more prolonged by anticoagulation, with hypertension as a contributor.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

model.text: Hello, Mr Penn, I’m Dr Clarke. What can I do for you today?

I keep getting nosebleeds, doctor. Several over the past few weeks. The last one was a real worry, it wouldn’t stop for a good twenty minutes and there was a fair bit of blood. I’m on a blood thinner, apixaban, for my irregular heartbeat — atrial fibrillation — and I take tablets for blood pressure. Should I be concerned?

That sounds frightening, especially the last one. I’d like to ask a few questions, look in your nose and check your blood pressure, then we’ll make a plan together. First, are you bleeding at all now, and do you feel faint or dizzy?
model.why: Checks for active bleeding and shock first

model.text: No, it’s stopped. I feel fine now.
When it bleeds, does it come from one side or both? And does blood run down the back of your throat?
Both sides at different times. Some went down my throat, but I had my head back.
What did you do to stop it?
I tipped my head back and held the top of my nose. I kept letting go to see if it had stopped.
Do you ever feel your nose blocked on one side, get blood-stained discharge, or pain or swelling in your face?
No, nothing like that.

Any bleeding elsewhere, like your gums, bruising easily, or blood in your urine or stools? And do you or anyone in your family have small red spots on the lips or fingers, or a family history of nosebleeds?
No. Nothing like that in the family either.
Which blood thinner are you on? Is it warfarin with INR checks, or one of the newer ones? And do you take aspirin or anti-inflammatory painkillers as well?
model.why: Identifies anticoagulant type and interacting drugs

model.text: Apixaban — the one without the blood tests. It’s for my atrial fibrillation. Nothing else on top.
That’s fine, I’ll look on your record. Have the bleeds made you stop taking it, or miss any doses?
No, I’ve kept taking it. I didn’t know if I should.
What’s been going through your mind about these bleeds?
I worry it means something’s wrong inside. And with the thinners, I worry one day it won’t stop.
Those are sensible worries. What were you hoping we’d do today?
Just to know whether I should worry, and how to stop them.

Let me check your pulse and blood pressure, then look inside the front of your nose with a light … There’s no bleeding right now. I’m looking for a small blood vessel at the front of the middle wall of the nose, which is where most nosebleeds come from.
So is it serious?

Most nosebleeds, even on blood thinners, come from that area at the front and aren’t dangerous. The thinner doesn’t cause them, but it makes them last longer. So the plan is to stop them happening, stop them faster when they do, and check your medicines and blood pressure.
model.why: Explains anterior source and anticoagulant effect proportionately

model.text: That’s a relief.

The first thing is first aid, because the way most people are taught is wrong. Sit up and lean forward, not back. Pinch the soft part of your nose, here below the bone, firmly for a full 10 to 15 minutes by the clock, without letting go to check. Spit out any blood. Could you show me how you’d do it?
model.why: Teaches correct first aid and checks by demonstration

model.text: Like this? Lean forward, pinch here, don’t let go.

Perfect. If it’s still bleeding after that, do it once more. If it won’t stop after that second go, or blood pours down your throat, or you feel faint or sweaty, go to A&E, and call 999 if you feel unwell. On a blood thinner we don’t wait around.
Should I stop the blood thinner?

Please don’t stop it yourself. It protects you from something serious. I’ll review why you’re on it — your atrial fibrillation — and check the apixaban dose against your age, kidney tests and weight; it doesn’t need INR checks like warfarin. If we need to change anything, I’ll discuss it with whoever looks after your heart.
Okay. And my blood pressure?

I’ll use today’s reading and a few home readings to see if it needs adjusting, because higher pressure can make bleeds worse. For the recurrences, if I can see a vessel at the front I can seal it with a special stick, and an antiseptic cream inside the nostril helps it heal. Keep the inside of your nose moist with saline spray or a smear of petroleum jelly, and avoid picking or blowing hard. If they carry on despite that, I’ll refer you to the ENT team.
model.why: BP, cautery, nasal cream, prevention and ENT referral

model.text: That all sounds sensible.

Come back sooner if the bleeds become one-sided with a blocked nose, you notice bruising or bleeding elsewhere, or they keep coming despite all this. I’ll see you in two weeks with your blood pressure readings and results. Can you tell me the plan in your own words?
Lean forward, pinch the soft bit for 15 minutes without peeking, A&E if it won’t stop or I feel faint. Keep taking the thinner. Cream and saline, and back in two weeks.
That’s exactly right. You were right to take it seriously.

social.t: Ask who is around if a big bleed happens and whether he could get to A&E. Anxiety about bleeds can make people stop medicines secretly.
Central heating and dry air worsen crusting; simple humidification and nasal moisturisers help.

legal.t: If a specialist started the anticoagulant, changes should be agreed with them. Document the discussion, the bleeding history and the risk-benefit reasoning.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain benefits and risks of nasal cautery (discomfort, rarely septal perforation with repeated bilateral cautery) before proceeding.

professional.t: Recurrent bleeding on an anticoagulant is a trigger for a structured medication review: indication, dose, renal function, interactions, adherence.
Only perform cautery if trained and the bleeding point is visible; otherwise refer to ENT.

community.t: Community pharmacists can check for interacting over-the-counter medicines such as NSAIDs; anticoagulation clinics manage INR if on warfarin.

redFlags: Bleeding not controlled by two rounds of correct pressure
Posterior bleed: blood down the throat, both nostrils, no anterior source
Persistent one-sided bleeding with nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pain or mass (sinonasal tumour)
Bleeding elsewhere or easy bruising; telangiectasia or family history (HHT)
psychosocial: Fear that a bleed on thinners won’t stop
Uncertainty about whether to keep taking the anticoagulant
Who is at home to help
ice: Concern: a bleed that won’t stop on blood thinners
Expectation: to know whether to worry and how to stop them

playbook.diagnosis: “These are recurrent nosebleeds from the front of the nose. Your blood thinner makes them last longer, and blood pressure may add to it, but they’re usually not a sign of something sinister.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Just inside the front of the nose there’s a spot where lots of tiny blood vessels meet, close to the surface. When the lining dries and cracks, one breaks. The blood thinner doesn’t cause the crack, it just slows the plug forming, so pressing properly for long enough gives it time to seal.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this means something serious inside and that a bleed might not stop. Most come from the front of the nose and aren’t dangerous, and I’ll give you the exact steps and the exact point to go to hospital.”
management.psychosocial: Correct the technique by demonstration; reassure that continuing the anticoagulant is right while it is reviewed; check he could get help quickly.
sharedPlan: Anticoagulant review: indication, dose, renal function, INR if warfarin, interacting drugs; no self-stopping
BP check and home readings; optimise per NICE NG136
Cautery if a visible anterior vessel and trained; antiseptic nasal cream (per BNF); saline or petroleum jelly for dryness
ENT referral if recurrent despite treatment
safetyNet: A&E if not stopped after two rounds of 10–15 minutes’ pressure, blood pouring down the throat, or faintness; 999 if unwell
Urgent review for one-sided obstruction, discharge or facial swelling, or bleeding elsewhere
Review in two weeks with BP readings and results

pitfalls.intro: The dangerous mistakes here are stopping the anticoagulant, leaving poor first aid uncorrected, and giving no clear point to go to hospital.

items.fail: Advising him to stop or pause the anticoagulant.
items.why: The bleeding is usually anterior and manageable; stopping exposes him to stroke or clot risk.
items.fix: Keep taking it; review indication, dose, renal function, INR if warfarin and interactions; agree any change with the prescriber.

items.fail: Describing first aid without checking what he actually does.
items.why: He tips his head back and lets go to check, which is why bleeds last.
items.fix: Ask him to show you, then correct it: lean forward, soft part, 10–15 minutes by the clock.

items.why: An anticoagulated man with a prolonged bleed needs a clear threshold for A&E.
items.fix: Two rounds of correct pressure, blood down the throat, or faintness means A&E; 999 if unwell.

items.fail: Not asking about one-sided obstruction, bleeding elsewhere or HHT features.
items.why: These change the diagnosis to sinonasal tumour, a bleeding disorder or HHT.
items.fix: Three quick questions and a look at the lips and fingers.

items.why: He had a frightening bleed; brisk reassurance ignores his concern.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear, then explain why most are anterior and what makes them safer.

items.fail: Ending without a check that he understood the technique or the plan.
items.why: Non-specific closure is common failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back of first aid, the A&E trigger and the follow-up date.

timeMap.d: Open question, then check he is not bleeding or faint now.
Side, blood down the throat, current first-aid technique, one-sided obstruction, bleeding elsewhere, HHT, which anticoagulant, antiplatelets or NSAIDs, missed doses.
Fear something is wrong inside and that a bleed won’t stop.
Pulse, BP, anterior rhinoscopy; most bleeds are anterior; thinners prolong, don’t cause.
Teach and check first aid, escalation, anticoagulant and BP review, cautery or cream, prevention, ENT if recurrent, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Tells him to stop his anticoagulant; never corrects the head-back, bony-bridge technique; no criteria for when to go to hospital; ignores his blood pressure.
wordPics.pass: Teaches correct first aid, reviews the anticoagulant and BP, gives clear A&E criteria, and offers cream or cautery with ENT referral if bleeds recur.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks him to demonstrate the technique; checks for one-sided obstruction, bleeding elsewhere and HHT; identifies the anticoagulant, INR if warfarin, and interacting drugs; reassures proportionately about his fear; uses teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Stop your blood thinner until the nosebleeds settle.”
avoid.instead: “Please keep taking it. I’ll review it and discuss any change with your heart team.”
avoid.why: Stopping an anticoagulant without review exposes him to stroke or clot risk.

avoid.instead: “Lean forward and pinch the soft part for a full 10 to 15 minutes without letting go.”
avoid.why: Head-back and bony-bridge pinching are ineffective and make him swallow blood.

For the recurrences, if I can see a vessel at the front I can seal it with a special stick, and an antiseptic cream inside the nostril helps it heal. Keep the inside of your nose moist with saline spray or a smear of petroleum jelly, and avoid picking or blowing hard. If they carry on despite that, I’ll refer you to the ENT team.
SCA_MODELS.why: BP, cautery, nasal cream, prevention and ENT referral

SCA_MODELS.text: That all sounds sensible.

Come back sooner if the bleeds become one-sided with a blocked nose, you notice bruising or bleeding elsewhere, or they keep coming despite all this. I’ll see you in two weeks with your blood pressure readings and results. Can you tell me the plan in your own words?
Lean forward, pinch the soft bit for 15 minutes without peeking, A&E if it won’t stop or I feel faint. Keep taking the thinner. Cream and saline, and back in two weeks.
That’s exactly right. You were right to take it seriously.

SCA_STEM.reason: Several nosebleeds over the past few weeks; the latest took about twenty minutes to stop.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG136 (hypertension in adults) · [2] Curaçao criteria for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Shovlin et al., 2000, international) · [3] Second international HHT guidelines (Faughnan et al., Ann Intern Med 2020, international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Most recurrent nosebleeds come from Little’s area at the front of the septum and are benign, but anticoagulation makes them last longer. Teach first aid properly, review the anticoagulant and blood pressure without stopping the anticoagulant on impulse, treat a visible anterior vessel, and know when to send to hospital. Keep one-sided bleeding with obstruction, and HHT, in mind.

points.t: Sit up and lean forward, mouth open. Pinch the soft, fleshy part of the nose (not the bony bridge) firmly and continuously for 10–15 minutes without letting go to check. Spit out blood rather than swallow it. A cold pack on the bridge may help. Afterwards avoid blowing, picking, straining, heavy lifting and hot drinks for a day or so.

The large majority arise anteriorly from Little’s area. Triggers include dryness, picking, trauma and colds. Posterior bleeds are more likely in older people, those on anticoagulants and those with hypertension: blood pouring down the throat, bleeding from both nostrils, or no visible anterior source.

Same-day emergency care (999 if unwell) if bleeding continues despite 10–15 minutes of correct pressure repeated once, is heavy or posterior, or there are signs of shock: pallor, sweating, dizziness, faintness, fast pulse, low blood pressure. A low threshold applies when anticoagulated.

points.h: Review the anticoagulant, don’t just stop it
points.t: Check the indication and whether it is still needed, the dose against current weight and renal function (DOACs), interacting drugs (antiplatelets, NSAIDs), and INR if on warfarin. Stopping or pausing an anticoagulant is a shared decision with the prescriber or specialist, weighed against stroke or clot risk.
Measure BP. Hypertension is associated with epistaxis severity; optimise control per NICE NG136 [1]. A very high reading during a bleed may partly reflect distress; recheck.

If a bleeding point is visible anteriorly and the clinician is trained, silver nitrate cautery to one side of the septum. Chlorhexidine with neomycin nasal cream reduces crusting and re-bleeding (dose per BNF; Naseptin contains arachis oil, so check for peanut or soya allergy). Refer to ENT when bleeds keep recurring despite this, or no source is seen.

Persistent one-sided bleeding with nasal obstruction, blood-stained discharge, facial pain or swelling, or a visible mass: refer urgently to ENT to exclude a sinonasal tumour. Easy bruising or other bleeding: FBC and clotting. HHT: recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds, telangiectasia on lips, tongue or fingers, and a first-degree relative with HHT [2][3].

Treat dryness (saline spray, a thin smear of petroleum jelly or emollient inside the nostril, humidifying the room), stop picking and forceful blowing, and address contributing medicines such as NSAIDs.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; checked straight away for active bleeding and faintness; let him describe the twenty-minute bleed.
Worry about the blood thinner and whether he should keep taking it; how the bleeds affect him.
Picked up “wouldn’t stop for twenty minutes” and blood down the throat as possible severity markers; corrected the head-back technique.
Idea (something wrong inside), concern (a bleed that won’t stop on thinners), expectation (whether to worry, how to stop them).
Pulse and BP; anterior rhinoscopy for a bleeding point; FBC and renal function (apixaban dosing) as indicated; INR only if on warfarin.
Anterior Little’s area bleed versus posterior bleed, anticoagulant effect, hypertension, bleeding disorder, HHT, sinonasal tumour.
Screened shock, one-sided obstruction or discharge, bleeding elsewhere and HHT features.
Recurrent anterior epistaxis made more prolonged by anticoagulation, with hypertension as a contributor.
Correct first aid taught and demonstrated; escalation criteria; cautery and antiseptic cream; prevention; ENT if recurrent.
Anticoagulant reviewed (indication, dose, INR if warfarin, interactions) without advising him to stop; BP optimisation per NICE NG136.
A&E or 999 for uncontrolled bleeding or faintness; return for one-sided symptoms or bleeding elsewhere; review in two weeks; teach-back.

social.t: Ask who is around if a big bleed happens and whether he could get to A&E. Anxiety about bleeds can make people stop medicines secretly.
Central heating and dry air worsen crusting; simple humidification and nasal moisturisers help.

legal.t: If a specialist started the anticoagulant, changes should be agreed with them. Document the discussion, the bleeding history and the risk-benefit reasoning.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain benefits and risks of nasal cautery (discomfort, rarely septal perforation with repeated bilateral cautery) before proceeding.

professional.t: Recurrent bleeding on an anticoagulant is a trigger for a structured medication review: indication, dose, renal function, interactions, adherence.
Only perform cautery if trained and the bleeding point is visible; otherwise refer to ENT.

community.t: Community pharmacists can check for interacting over-the-counter medicines such as NSAIDs; anticoagulation clinics manage INR if on warfarin.

redFlags: Bleeding not controlled by two rounds of correct pressure
Posterior bleed: blood down the throat, both nostrils, no anterior source
Persistent one-sided bleeding with nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pain or mass (sinonasal tumour)
Bleeding elsewhere or easy bruising; telangiectasia or family history (HHT)
psychosocial: Fear that a bleed on thinners won’t stop
Uncertainty about whether to keep taking the anticoagulant
Who is at home to help
ice: Concern: a bleed that won’t stop on blood thinners
Expectation: to know whether to worry and how to stop them

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “These are recurrent nosebleeds from the front of the nose. Your blood thinner makes them last longer, and blood pressure may add to it, but they’re usually not a sign of something sinister.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Just inside the front of the nose there’s a spot where lots of tiny blood vessels meet, close to the surface. When the lining dries and cracks, one breaks. The blood thinner doesn’t cause the crack, it just slows the plug forming, so pressing properly for long enough gives it time to seal.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this means something serious inside and that a bleed might not stop. Most come from the front of the nose and aren’t dangerous, and I’ll give you the exact steps and the exact point to go to hospital.”
management.psychosocial: Correct the technique by demonstration; reassure that continuing the anticoagulant is right while it is reviewed; check he could get help quickly.
sharedPlan: Anticoagulant review: indication, dose, renal function, INR if warfarin, interacting drugs; no self-stopping
BP check and home readings; optimise per NICE NG136
Cautery if a visible anterior vessel and trained; antiseptic nasal cream (per BNF); saline or petroleum jelly for dryness
ENT referral if recurrent despite treatment
safetyNet: A&E if not stopped after two rounds of 10–15 minutes’ pressure, blood pouring down the throat, or faintness; 999 if unwell
Urgent review for one-sided obstruction, discharge or facial swelling, or bleeding elsewhere
Review in two weeks with BP readings and results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The dangerous mistakes here are stopping the anticoagulant, leaving poor first aid uncorrected, and giving no clear point to go to hospital.

items.fail: Advising him to stop or pause the anticoagulant.
items.why: The bleeding is usually anterior and manageable; stopping exposes him to stroke or clot risk.
items.fix: Keep taking it; review indication, dose, renal function, INR if warfarin and interactions; agree any change with the prescriber.

items.fail: Describing first aid without checking what he actually does.
items.why: He tips his head back and lets go to check, which is why bleeds last.
items.fix: Ask him to show you, then correct it: lean forward, soft part, 10–15 minutes by the clock.

items.why: An anticoagulated man with a prolonged bleed needs a clear threshold for A&E.
items.fix: Two rounds of correct pressure, blood down the throat, or faintness means A&E; 999 if unwell.

items.fail: Not asking about one-sided obstruction, bleeding elsewhere or HHT features.
items.why: These change the diagnosis to sinonasal tumour, a bleeding disorder or HHT.
items.fix: Three quick questions and a look at the lips and fingers.

items.why: He had a frightening bleed; brisk reassurance ignores his concern.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear, then explain why most are anterior and what makes them safer.

items.fail: Ending without a check that he understood the technique or the plan.
items.why: Non-specific closure is common failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back of first aid, the A&E trigger and the follow-up date.
